name: George Lindsay D'Arcy

notes:
SUDDEN DEATH OF MR. G. L.
D'ARCY.
'When Mr. George Lindsay 'D'Arcy, who is
a clerk in the correspondence branch of the
Home Secretary's Department, was alight-
ing from a tram near the Treasury Build-
ing on Saturday morning, either as it was
' stopping or had stopped, he was seen to fall
heavily backwards, striking his head on
the wood paving. He was picked up in an
I unconscious condition, and conveyed,into

Mr. Corinack's chemist shop. Dr. Hopkins
and the Ambulance were summoned,
and it was ascertained that Mr. D'Arcy had
sustained a severe scalp wound, which was
jat once dressed under the doctor's direcections.
He was then conveyed to
his home in Sussex - street, South
Brisbane, and left in the care of Dr.
Webb. A message was shortly afterwards
received at the office that he had died.
He was well advanced in years, being 71
years of age, and leaves a widow and
grown-up family. Mr. D'Arcy was a well
liked and esteemed old member of the civil
service. He entered the Government em-
ploy as far back as 1st April, 1863, as
Clerk of the Executive Council, but a year
later was placed in the correspondence
branch of the Home Secretary's Depart-
ment, where he has remained ever since.
He was given some letters on Friday to
draft, and these were found on Saturday
done in pencil," with the quotation, " Dust
thou art, to dust returnest," written at the
, bottom of the paper. In view of the
sad occurrence next morning, this incident
is singular. Saturday was Mrs. D'Arcy''s
birthday, and possibly the certain amount
of mild excitement induced by the circum-
stance may have been the primary cause
of the collapse, as the deceased gentleman
made himself fairly busy on Friday select-
ing those presents by which he and the
members of his family thought fit to cele-
brate the birthday of the partner of his
declining years. He was buried, in the
South Brisbane Cemetery yesterday after-
noon.

OBITUARY

 

"At Parramatta, on Suuday morning, the 22nd of July, 1849, aged 69, Major George Pitt D'Arcy, formerly of the 39th Regiment of Foot; a braye and gallant soldier. Major D'Arcy served In the West Indies, the Mediterranean, through the whole of the Peninsular War, South America, and In this colony. He received a medal for commanding his regment nt tile battle of Ortbes."

 

This is the brief announcement of the death of one who was every inch a soldier, and whose memory will long be preserved in the hearts of those who knew him for being the possessor of nought but good and kindly qualities. The decline of a life spent iu the service of his country, was not, we deeply regret to say, passed in the paths of pleasantness; and though philosophy taught Major D'Arcy to sustain sorrow and trouble uncomplainingly-although his high spirit never quailed beneath the frowns of the world--although, while drinking deeply of the waters of Marah, his sung and tale were I wont "to set the table in it roar," yet those who were intimately ncquaimed with him had reason to know that the canker of disappointment was at "his heart's care," and his smile was, tuo often, only the shroud of buried hopes.

 

 

 

 

He died at the house of Mr. Walford, one of his staunchest friends, whose kindness to the deceased gentleman increased in proportion to his need of it. From the suddenness of his death, it was deemed uecessary to hold a« inquest over his body.

 

The result was, that the jury returned a verdict imputing the cause of his decease !lo "gout which had flown to the heady ] and caused apoplexy." ?] . -i'

 

In Major D'Arcy the colony has lost a gallant spirit, one who in hit lifetime tried to be the friend of all, and never injured anyone but himself.

 

The following is an epitome of thc Major's services:-

 

"In the West Indies, North and South America, Mediterranean, and in the Peninsular under his Grace the Duke of Wellington-from the year 1811 until the conclusion of the war after the battle of Toulouse.

 

He was present in tbe following actions

 

Victoria, 2nd in command

 

Nivelle, 2nd in command

 

Nive, 2nd in command

 

Pyrenees, 2nd in command

 

Orthes, commanded

 

Toulouse, 3rd in command

 

He was also engaged with the enemy in their retreat from the battle of Pampeluna; also at Aire, anil at the affair of Garisse, on which occasion the Duke of Wellington in his dispatch mentioned the 39th Regiment as having distinguished itself.

 

The command fell to Major D'Arcy, in consequence of Lt-Colonel Bruce being wounded early in the action. The Major received a gold medal for his prominent services in the battle of Orthes, but singular to relate, after a lapse of four years, the reward of his merit having been sent by mistake to Lt-Colonel Bruce. Major D'Arcy served 34 years in the 39th Regiment.

Robert D'ARCY Major-Gen C.B.

1 UPDA

2 PLAC Royal Engineers

2 SOUR S32

A lineal descendant of the great and ancient baronial house of D'Arcy, in

which vested the Earldom of Holderness. (SEE NOES FOR THE 4TH EARL - THIS ROBERT THOUGHT TO BE THE ILLEGITIMATE SON OF THE 4TH EARL AND NOT OF FRANCIS) He was born in Yorkshire and spent his holidays in Holderness House London and was a friend of the Marquis Townsend.

Mystery about his father but the College of Heralds allow the family to carry the Arms of Lord D'Arcy, Earl of Holderness and Baron Conyers.

From "Ancestral Voices" by Berta Ruck

"We know that he was "wrecked" on his voyage to America to fight as a volunteer in the American war and that in this wreck personal papers including, birth certificate and documents with the names of his parents were lost. It was rumoured (not through family letters) but handed down talk that the loss of these personal papers was engineered to avoid a possible scandal.

The Yorkshire Myth - by rights perhaps he was not of that branch of the D'Arcy family - he had been taken on by them for some unexplained reason to PASS as their child."

GAK D'A wrote " from a variety of circumstantial evidence I am inclined to believe that the General (Robert) was an illegitimate son of the last Earl of Holderness who died in 1788. The name Robert - The general having been born and educated in Yorkshire, passing his holidays in Holderness House, London. His silence about his father, of whom he never spoke.

His powerful friend, the Marquiss of Townshend, a relation of Earl Holderness, taking him by the hand - and making much of him. My father saying he never knew who his grandfather was - One of his sons being named Considine, a family name with the Yorkshire D'Arcys."

There is also a letter to GAKD'A from his cousin Frederick in Australia "your excellent father (J. D'Arcy) gave me to understand before he left England that the title of Holderness had been traced to you, or rather to the General (Robert) who was then alive. I think your father touched up a little by your uncle De La Warr, (Lady Catherine's dearest brother) thought of applying to Chancery but considered that he was not of sufficient financial calibre.

I believe caviats are invited and always entered by Parties having spurious claims merely to exact tips. However I look upon you (George A K D'A) as the Earl of Holderness proper."

If any of this is to be believed then Robert would be direct link to the 4th Earl and we would not be looking for the Thomas or Francis (Soldier of Fortune).

Spain (Minorca)

During the last period of British occupation (1798–1802) of Minorca, Sir Charles Stuart, the then British governor, ordered Engineer Captain Robert D´Arcy to build some 12 Martello towers along the coast.[6] These, when added to the three Spanish towers already in place, gave Minorca 15 towers.[

The Harbour Control. Sa Torre de Sanitja. The figure of Sanitja Tower is a landmark standing at the entrance of the harbour that transmits a romantic feeling, one of remote militar and imperial times. It was built by the English in 1800, as part of a defensive network of 11 towers erected on the island’s most strategical points. The one at Sanitja was built by Captain Robert d'Arcy during the last period of British rule between 1798 and 1802, and it was prepared to house a garrison of 18 men with supplies for a month.

Its mission was to control and watch the area against possible pirates or French invasion expeditions. Its defense was vital for the communitacion system that used smoke signals during the day and fire at night, and that could be seen from El Toro Mountain or from a second Tower in the harbour of Fornells.

Robert Darcy, 3rd Earl of Holderness, PC (24 November 1681 – 20 January 1721) was a British peer and politician.

Darcy was the second (but eldest surviving) son of John Darcy, Lord Conyers, himself the eldest son of Conyers Darcy, 2nd Earl of Holderness. He was styled Lord Conyers when his father died in 1688 and later inherited his grandfather's earldom in 1692. He also inherited the titles of 10th Baron Darcy de Knayth and 7th Baron Conyers. In 1698 he matriculated fellow-commoner from King's College, Cambridge.[1] In 1714, the Earl of Holderness, as he now was, was appointed Lord Lieutenant of the North Riding of Yorkshire and admitted to the Privy Council and appointed First Lord of Trade in 1718. He was also a Lord of the Bedchamber from 1719 to his death.

On 26 May 1715, Holderness had married Lady Frederica Schomberg (the eldest surviving daughter of the 3rd Duke of Schomberg) and they had two surviving children: Hon. Robert (1718–1778) and Lady Caroline (d. 1778, married the 4th Marquess of Lothian).

On Lord Holderness' death in 1721, his title passed to his only surviving son, Robert, and his wife later married the future 1st Earl FitzWalter.
